query: For a titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state, whose elevated-temperature mechanical performance remains unestablished when titanium and nickel serve as primary constituents rather than additions, what single testable intervention hypothesis could produce better mechanical properties under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing than the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, mechanism, predicted relative outcome, applicable composition and test-regime boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of yttrium to a titanium–nickel based high-entropy alloy will induce the in situ formation of fine yttrium oxide dispersoids that enhance its high‐temperature strength and creep resistance compared to the unmodified alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase solid-solution high-entropy alloy in which titanium and nickel are the primary constituents, exhibiting a homogeneous microstructure without significant secondary phases.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled minor addition (e.g., 0.5–1 wt%) of yttrium during alloy fabrication.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing in elevated-temperature regimes (approximately 700–1000°C) and in environments that simulate extreme oxidation or reactive conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a fine, evenly distributed dispersion of yttrium oxide (Y2O3) nanoprecipitates within the alloy matrix.
generation.mechanism: Yttrium reacts with residual oxygen during processing or subsequent thermal exposure to form stable nano-oxides, which act as obstacles to dislocation motion and grain boundary sliding, thereby enhancing yield strength and creep resistance at high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under the specified high-temperature and extreme environmental conditions, the yttrium-modified alloy will exhibit improved yield strength and slower creep deformation rates compared to the same alloy produced without yttrium.
generation.baseline: The identical titanium–nickel based high-entropy alloy produced without any yttrium addition.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to alloys where titanium and nickel are the main constituents and is valid for testing regimes in the elevated temperature range (700–1000°C) under conditions where oxidation or environmental degradation is a concern.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of mechanical property improvement (e.g., percentage increase in yield strength and creep resistance) is uncertain and requires experimental validation. Additionally, the stability and distribution of the nano-oxides over prolonged high-temperature exposure remain to be confirmed.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of alloy samples with identical compositions except that one set includes a 0.5–1 wt% addition of yttrium. Subject both sample sets to identical heat-treatment processes and then perform mechanical testing in the temperature range of 700–1000°C, along with microstructural analyses (e.g., TEM) to verify the presence and stability of yttrium oxide dispersoids.
measurements: High-temperature tensile tests to determine yield strength and ultimate tensile strength
Creep tests to measure deformation rates and creep life
TEM or other high-resolution microscopy to assess the formation, size distribution, and stability of oxide dispersoids
Oxidation resistance tests under controlled reactive atmospheres
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the yttrium-modified alloy does not display statistically significant improvements in mechanical properties (i.e., yield strength, creep resistance, oxidation resistance) compared to the baseline alloy, or if microstructural analysis does not confirm the in situ formation of fine, well-dispersed yttrium oxide particles.
